tldr: AppWorld is a new benchmark with a controllable simulation engine of 9 everyday apps (457 APIs) and 750 complex tasks that require iterative code generation and multi-app interaction, exposing significant gaps in current LLM capabilities for autonomous agent tasks.
contributions: AppWorld Engine: a controllable, reproducible execution environment simulating 9 real-world apps via 457 APIs with ~100 fictitious users and 370K database rows
AppWorld Benchmark: 750 natural, diverse, challenging tasks requiring rich interactive code generation across multiple apps
Programmatic state-based evaluation suite with unit tests that check for goal completion and collateral damage
Benchmarking results showing GPT4-o solves only ~49% of normal and ~30% of challenge tasks
methods: The authors built AppWorld Engine using FastAPI, SQLite, and SQLModel ORM, implementing 9 apps (e.g., Amazon, Venmo, Gmail, Spotify) with 457 APIs that perform read/write operations on an underlying database. The Base DB was populated procedurally using simulated activities of ~106 fictitious users aged 19-60 with interpersonal relationships, supplemented by manual and ChatGPT-generated text entries. Tasks were generated via Task Scenarios with programmatically instantiated variations ensuring tasks are well-defined, contain distractors and hurdles, and form contrast sets. Evaluation uses state-based programmatic assertions checking database diffs between start and end states for goal completion and collateral damage.
results: GPT4-o with ReAct achieves 48.8% Task Goal Completion (TGC) on normal tasks and 30.2% on challenge tasks. GPT4-turbo-0613 scores 32.7% and 17.5% respectively. Under the stricter scenario-based robustness metric (SGC), GPT4-o drops to 32.1% and 13.0%. GPT4-o is the best-performing model tested, with other models scoring at least 16% fewer. Tasks average 1.8 apps and 9.5 APIs per task, with code averaging 50 lines (max 134). The benchmark contains 750 tasks with an average of 8 unit tests per task (max 22).
limitations: The benchmark was built over 14 months by a small subset of authors with NLP and software engineering experience (~100K lines of code), limiting reproducibility by other groups. Some data entries required manual generation (e.g., workout notes) or ChatGPT prompting, introducing potential biases. The evaluation checks only expected and allowed database changes, which may not capture all forms of unintended behavior. The benchmark focuses on ~100 fictitious users with simulated activities, which may not fully represent the diversity of real-world digital environments.
